transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08 11:00 PT / 19:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Redwood CSM), Maya Kapoor (VenturerX Head of Platform), Ethan Ross (SRE Lead), Priya Nair (Security Architect)

Auto-summary: Customer evaluating reliability and incident tolerance for LLM inference. Key asks: deterministic tail latency, fallback strategies, private deploy networking constraints, and compliance docs.

[00:00:00] Avery Chen: All right, folks, welcome. thanks for taking the time. i'm avery on the redwood side, i'm the AE, with diego our SE. we'll run through how folks typically handle fallbacks and multi-region routing.
[00:00:18] Maya Kapoor: hey avery, thanks. quick context - we run a latency-sensitive recommendation API, 95th P95 target is ~220ms end-to-end, and we have some EU data residency plus SOC2 needs. evaluating hosted and whether dedicated or private gives us better guarantees.
[00:00:36] Diego Morales: got it, thanks maya. couple clarifying q's up front — is the 220ms including client-to-redwood network and model generation, or just inference window?
[00:00:46] Maya Kapoor: that's end-to-end from our api gateway to response back to the user — so yes full path.
[00:00:54] Ethan Ross: we also want predictable tail, not just avg. sudden spikes from longer sequences have bitten us before.
[00:01:05] Priya Nair: and from security side, if we go private we need KMS/HSM integrations, SSO with our okta, and audit logs stored for 2 years.
[00:01:15] Avery Chen: thanks, good constraints. we'll walk through typical fallback patterns: model downgrade to a smaller/quantized variant, traffic steering to another region, and partial degradation (e.g., truncated responses or cached stub answers). i'll hand off to diego to explain cost/latency tradeoffs.

[00:01:36] Diego Morales: yeah, so imagine three tiers: hosted (we run everything, fastest to onboard), dedicated (reserved pools for you -> more predictable throughput), private (control plane in your vpc or on-prem). For tail latency: dedicated gives stronger guarantees because you avoid noisy neighbor and can get reserved capacity; private — you can instrument network and use colocated infra for lowest variance.
[00:02:00] Diego Morales: fallback policies we recommend: primary: host model A in region-us-east; secondary: region-eu-west fallback; tertiary: downgrade model to A-small quantized with shorter max tokens. also automatic warm caches for common prefixes.
[00:02:20] Maya Kapoor: can you do automatic KV cache priming? we saw reference to prefix caching but not sure how it works at scale.
[00:02:29] Diego Morales: yes, we do prefix and KV cache— the runtime keeps token-level KV to avoid recompute, and you can pin warm keys. there's also a cache-priming API to pre-populate based on expected prompts. sometimes the transcript generator will lose the casing — we call it K V cache in docs, sorry about that.
[00:02:46] Ethan Ross: if region fails, how fast is steering? like at the DNS level or application? what about in-flight requests?
[00:02:55] Diego Morales: we do smart routing in the control plane. steering is immediate for new requests; in-flight we attempt graceful fallback: if it's in the KV warm path we'll try a regional mirrored replica, otherwise we can failover to the downgrade model. there's also a circuit breaker you can tune that fails fast to avoid long tails.
[00:03:12] Priya Nair: about audit logs — can we ship logs to our s3 and retain 2 years? encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS?
[00:03:20] Lina Park: yes, for private and dedicated we support customer KMS + audit log routing to your bucket or SIEM, we also have built-in retention policies. for hosted there are options but we recommend dedicated/private for strict residency.

[00:03:40] Maya Kapoor: what's the SLA you offer for hosted? i've seen marketing but wanted specifics for production-readiness.
[00:03:47] Avery Chen: hosted has a standard 99.9% availability for the API in our docs; dedicated has SLA tiers up to 99.95 with reserved pools and 24/7 support. private SLA is contract-defined but can be pushed to 99.99 with hot-standby options. keep in mind availability is different from latency SLOs — we can commit to uptime but tail latency needs sizing.
[00:04:08] Ethan Ross: so if we set a P95 target of 220ms, do you size a dedicated pool? what's the formal acceptance criteria?
[00:04:16] Diego Morales: typically we run a sizing bench: you give us request distribution + sequence lengths; we simulate with your target model and OS/quant profiles. acceptance criteria often include hitting P95 and 99th thresholds under 1.25x expected traffic. we can run a short pilot with traffic mirroring.
[00:04:34] Maya Kapoor: traffic mirroring sounds good — will it cost a lot?
[00:04:39] Diego Morales: mirror is free-ish in terms of profiling, but if you run live inference at volume there are host compute costs. we can mirror a sample of traffic at peak windows for meaningful numbers.

[00:04:56] Priya Nair: private deploy — network constraints: we have strict egress rules, and only ports 443 to our proxy are allowed. can redwood control plane still manage agent heartbeats?
[00:05:07] Diego Morales: yes, private is designed for restrictive environments. the agent initiates outbound only, over TLS to control plane endpoints. some customers also run an air-gapped variant with an on-prem control plane.
[00:05:18] Maya Kapoor: what's the time to fall back to a quantized smaller model? i.e. latency added to a request that triggers downgrade mid-request.
[00:05:27] Diego Morales: if mid-request you generally don't switch model mid-stream; we fail fast and reissue to the smaller model, so you'll pay an extra request RTT. that said, if we detect tail risk earlier we proactively route to smaller model for new requests. typical extra cost is one roundtrip plus model generation time on the small model — maybe 50-150ms depending on sequence length.

[00:05:48] Ethan Ross: hmm, 50-150ms might push us over the 220ms 95th. tradeoff there. would a dedicated pool eliminate that?
[00:05:55] Diego Morales: dedicated reduces tail by avoiding noisy neighbors and with prewarmed workers you can reduce that reissue cost by keeping the smaller model hot. also using regional mirrors reduces network RTT.
[00:06:06] Maya Kapoor: can we do hybrid: hosted for burst/POC, dedicated for steady traffic, private for regulated EU subset?
[00:06:15] Avery Chen: absolutely, that's a common pattern. you can set routing policies: route EU traffic to private EU cluster, US to dedicated, and failover to hosted as a last resort. policies can be priority-based and also cost-aware.

[00:06:30] Priya Nair: any limitations on SSO for private? we use import SAML assertions and want RBAC mapped back to AD groups.
[00:06:38] Lina Park: we support SAML with group claims mapping. for private we can integrate to your IDP. RBAC can be synced to AD group names and you can control role-level permissions.

[00:06:52] Maya Kapoor: what about churn and deployments — we need canary rollouts so new model versions don't degrade latency unexpectedly.
[00:06:59] Diego Morales: rollouts are supported: canary splits, A/B, and automatic fallback if quality/latency regressions exceed thresholds. you can bind eval sets and Prometheus metrics to trigger automatic rollback.

[00:07:18] Ethan Ross: ok can we talk incident scenarios — e.g., region e-e outage during peak — what's the expected user impact and how do you recommend we reduce blast radius?
[00:07:28] Diego Morales: multi-region: primary region handles X% traffic. if region down, routing policy shifts to secondary. to reduce blast radius: 1) geo-split sticky sessions so critical users are pinned to regional replicas, 2) reserve burst capacity in secondary region (warm standby), 3) pre-populate caches in secondary. worst case we degrade responses (length or complexity) rather than full failure.
[00:07:54] Maya Kapoor: how do you test this? do you run chaos tests with customers?
[00:07:59] Avery Chen: some customers run joint chaos drills with Redwood — we can simulate region failovers in a staged test environment. we provide playbooks and runbooks for run-of-show.

[00:08:15] Priya Nair: for compliance we need signed runbooks and SOC evidence that we followed drills. is that something you provide?
[00:08:22] Lina Park: yes, we can provide drill reports and attestations for enterprise contracts and include runbook artifacts.

[00:08:35] Ethan Ross: on the network side — if we accept private deployment in EU, what bandwidth are typical for peak? our model payloads are ~1.2k tokens average.
[00:08:45] Diego Morales: bandwidth is mostly token streaming and kv cache warmups. for 1.2k tokens average and your QPS, we can estimate. if you share QPS numbers we'll produce a bandwidth and throughput calculator.

[00:08:58] Maya Kapoor: a thought — could we do local inference for the top-50 flows (hot intents) and remote for others? hybrid caching.
[00:09:07] Diego Morales: yep, edge caching + local lightweight models is common. Redwood's routing layer supports traffic steering to edge inference or central pools based on intent detection.

[00:09:20] Maya Kapoor: ok, let's talk about cost. if we reserve 4 GPUs in dedicated in us-east and 2 in eu-west vs hosted, ballpark difference?
[00:09:29] Diego Morales: rough rule: dedicated reserved capacity can be 30-50% cheaper per token at scale vs hosted, but there's commit cost. we'll share a spreadsheet that models your traffic. for your peaks we might recommend mixing reserved baseline + burst to hosted to optimize cost.

[00:09:45] Ethan Ross: another practical: how do fallbacks surface in our logs? we need to correlate a fallback event with request id for postmortem.
[00:09:54] Lina Park: every request has a tokenized event trail: routing decision, model version, fallback reason code. you can forward those to your observability stack.

[00:10:06] Priya Nair: are the reason codes standardized? we want machine-readable codes to alert.
[00:10:11] Diego Morales: yes, something like FBD-REGION-FAIL, FBD-MODEL-TIMEOUT, FBD-CB-TRIPPED; you can map them to alerts.

[00:10:23] Maya Kapoor: what's the recommended SLA clause language for a contract about degradations? we cant promise zero impact but want limits.
[00:10:30] Avery Chen: customers usually write SLO language: availability % for API + latency thresholds for P95/P99. fallback is documented as graceful degradation and explicitly excluded from uptime if it's a policy-based downgrade; but we include response-level SLOs for dedicated/private pilots as part of the contract.

[00:10:48] Ethan Ross: any required changes to client SDKs to handle fallbacks? we use our own gateway.
[00:10:53] Diego Morales: generally SDK changes are minimal — we recommend using idempotency keys for retries and honoring response headers that indicate fallback. for more advanced behavior we provide libs but since you have a gateway it's straightforward.

[00:11:06] Maya Kapoor: last question on demos — can we run a 2-week pilot where we mirror 10% of traffic and exercise a simulated eu region outage to observe behavior?
[00:11:15] Avery Chen: yes, pilot + chaos test is doable. diego will scope costs.

[00:11:25] Diego Morales: i'll need sample traffic and target windows. ideally we mirror a representative slice and run a scripted failover during non-peak initially.

[00:11:36] Priya Nair: concerning keys, if we use customer-managed KMS, will Redwood ever hold a copy of the keys?
[00:11:42] Lina Park: no, we integrate to your KMS; keys remain in your account for private/dedicated. hosted can use customer-managed keys with restrictions. we can share an architecture diagram.

[00:11:55] Maya Kapoor: perfect. can you also include a failure-mode matrix mapping to user-visible impact? that helps our legal and product teams.

[00:12:01] Avery Chen: sure — diego and lina will put together a matrix: failure mode, likelihood, user impact, mitigation, rollback playbook.

[00:12:10] Ethan Ross: one more nit — what's the cold-start for models on dedicated after autoscale if we get a sudden 3x spike?
[00:12:18] Diego Morales: autoscale has step-based increments, cold-start depends on GPU type and model size; for large models could be several seconds to tens of seconds. we mitigate with burst capacity, prewarmed workers, and predictive scaling hooks tied to traffic signals.

[00:12:33] Maya Kapoor: okay, wrap up church. (laughs)
[00:12:36] Avery Chen: quick recap from redwood side: we'll share cost matrix, runbook/DR playbook, SOC2+KMS docs, and propose dates for private-deploy deep-dive. venturerx to share traffic samples and compliance constraints. agreed on a pilot with 10% mirror + failover test.

[00:12:55] Priya Nair: thanks everyone. appreciate the thoroughness.
[00:12:59] Maya Kapoor: thanks. we'll wait for the email.

[00:13:04] Avery Chen: thanks, talk soon.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had occasional mis-typed acronyms (KV cache -> K V cache), some punctuation missing, speaker overlap around 00:05:00-00:06:30.
questions: How fast is region steering and what happens to in-flight requests?
Can Redwood integrate with our KMS and SAML/AD for private deploy?
What's the expected cost difference for reserved dedicated GPUs vs hosted at our scale?
